pages.text: The event finished, and the car park outside the hall emptied very quickly, the way car parks do when everyone leaves at the same time. Emeka, Sade, Isa, and Nosa were in the hall looking for Sade's jacket, which had been on her seat but was now elsewhere, and when they came back out, the minibus was gone. The jacket was found under a chair. The minibus was not found at all.

image.note: Illustration: an empty car park, four children standing looking at where the bus was, other cars still present

pages.text: Nosa's father had arranged for the family driver to collect him after the event. The driver believed Nosa's father was collecting him. Neither had confirmed this with the other. Both, at this moment, were doing something else entirely and not checking their phones.

Nosa called his father. No answer. He called the driver. No answer. He called his mother, who answered but was in Kaduna and could not help immediately beyond promising to keep trying his father. He looked at his phone. Fourteen percent battery. The venue staff were politely but clearly beginning to close the hall.

'We should think about this carefully,' Emeka said. Everyone agreed. They moved outside, away from the staff locking up, and sat on a low wall. Between the four of them they had enough money for one keke fare, not four. The estate was approximately three kilometres away. 'We know the route,' Isa said. 'Roughly,' Nosa said. 'Roughly is enough,' Emeka said, and opened his notebook.

Nosa sent one text to his mother: Driver mix-up. Walking home with Emeka Isa Sade. About 3km. Phone low battery. We are safe. Then he switched his phone to low power mode and put it in his pocket. It felt smaller than usual.

image.note: Illustration: the four children around Nosa's phone, Emeka writing something in his notebook

pages.text: 'Three kilometres,' Isa said. 'Forty minutes at a normal pace, less if we walk fast. We know the route is approximately north from here.' 'Approximately,' Sade said. 'We need landmarks,' Emeka said. 'Major roads. Things we can see from a distance. We use the water tower to the north as a bearing until we recognise more.' He wrote this down. 'My shoe is making a noise,' Sade said.
'My shoe is making a noise,' Sade said. Everyone looked at her shoe. The strap at the back was loose but still attached. 'It will probably be fine,' Nosa said. 'Probably,' Sade said. They walked.

They sat on the low wall and worked it out the way you work out any hard thing, which is slowly and without panic, because panic solves nothing and Emeka refused to allow it. Between the four of them they had one phone at fourteen percent and enough coins for a single keke fare, which was no use when there were four of them and no keke would take one child and leave three. The venue staff were kind but they were locking up, and kindness with a set of keys in its hand cannot help you for long.

So the choices narrowed, the way choices do, until only one was left. Home was three kilometres roughly north, along roads they half knew. On foot that was under an hour if they did not get lost, and getting lost was the only real risk, because the route was busy and lit and ordinary. It was not an adventure and Emeka was careful not to let anyone treat it as one. It was a problem with one sensible solution, and the sensible solution was to walk, together, carefully, and to tell someone first.

The first kilometre went well. They were on a main road they recognised and the junction at the bottom matched Emeka's notes. At the second junction, Isa was certain he knew which way to turn. He was wrong. They walked five minutes before a landmark resolved and they retraced their steps, which cost them more time than Emeka chose to calculate aloud.

image.note: Illustration: the four children pausing at a road junction looking at a distant landmark, Isa pointing confidently in the wrong direction

pages.text: 'Left,' Emeka said, when they were back at the junction. 'You said right,' Isa said. 'I said left and then I was uncertain and then I did not correct you when you said right,' Emeka said. 'That is different from saying right.'

They went left. Sade's shoe strap broke at the top of the hill. Not completely: one side held. She walked with it for a few hundred metres before they stopped and tied the broken strap to the intact one with a piece of string from the bottom of Emeka's school bag, which was the kind of school bag that contained string.

'Why do you have string in your bag?' Sade asked. 'String is useful,' Emeka said. He could not have said more clearly that he did not see this as a strange thing to need to explain. Sade looked at the repaired strap. It held. She looked at Emeka. 'Thank you for having string,' she said.

They walked north with the water tower ahead as their marker, and for the first kilometre it went well, and Emeka began, privately, to enjoy the neatness of it. Then, at the second junction, Isa said left with such confidence that everyone followed, and five minutes later a petrol station none of them recognised told them, without a word, that Isa had been wrong. Nobody blamed him out loud. They simply turned around and walked back, and Emeka noted the cost of the error in his head without saying the number, which was a kindness of a sort.

It was on the way back to the junction that Sade's shoe finally gave up, the strap parting at the heel with a small, final sound. She stood on one foot, holding the ruined shoe, and looked at it, and looked at Emeka, who was already unzipping the bottom pocket of his school bag, the one that contained, for reasons he did not consider strange, a length of string. He tied the strap to its own broken root while Sade balanced on his shoulder, and it held, and they walked on, slower now, but together.

They recognised the road the estate was on with about five minutes to go. The streetlights had come on while they were walking. The walk had taken just under an hour. Emeka noted the time in his notebook. Nosa noted that he had been more scared than he had let on, which was a thing he had been thinking about for the last ten minutes and now said out loud. Nobody said he shouldn't have been.

image.note: Illustration: four tired children on a familiar estate road at dusk, the estate gates visible in the distance

pages.text: Nosa's mother was at the estate gate. She had driven back from Kaduna faster than she should have, she said, and she did not say it as a complaint. Nosa's father arrived four minutes later, having just found the messages. He looked at Nosa. Nosa looked at him. 'The driver thought you were coming,' Nosa said. 'I know,' his father said. 'That is entirely my fault.' Sade's mother, who had been called by Nosa's mother, arrived at a run. She looked at Sade's shoe and said: 'What happened to your shoe?' Sade said: 'Emeka has string.'

At dinner, Emeka's father asked him to describe the route they had taken. Emeka described it in detail, including the wrong turn, which he described accurately and without omission. His father listened carefully. At the end, he said: 'The wrong turn cost you how long?' 'About ten minutes,' Emeka said. 'Would you make the same turn again?' 'No,' Emeka said. 'Good,' his father said. 'That is what mistakes are for.'

Nosa's father spoke to the driver the next morning. The conversation was brief and clear and not repeated. He also wrote himself a note, which he stuck to the dashboard of the car: Confirm collection. Every time. The four children had already moved on to the next thing, as children do. But Nosa kept his phone charged above fifty percent for the rest of the term, which was its own kind of lesson, and required no one to explain it to him.
